Hi Sara — thanks for the clear list. Short answers up front, followed by a short note on next steps: 

Short answers:
- Deletion semantics: a user-requested erasure creates a tombstone marker in our primary metadata store which flags the object as deleted. That marker is propagated asynchronously to backup/replica controllers; snapshots that are immutable at the time of snapshot creation retain the data until their configured TTL/expiration, but subsequent incremental backups will respect the tombstone.
- Legal hold: we support a legal hold flag at the account level. When enabled, GC/expunge jobs skip held objects regardless of TTL.
- KMS key destruction: if a customer-managed key is destroyed, any snapshots encrypted with that key become unrecoverable. We can provide key destruction audit logs, but we cannot decrypt or restore without the key.

Hi Sara — jumping in with the technical details you’ll need for the SOW. I’ve attached a short retention matrix and our DR playbook excerpt. Key points: 

1) Tombstone & propagation model- We write a tombstone marker to the metadata service at T0 (when deletion request is accepted). That marker is inserted into the changefeed and processed by our backup/replication controllers. Typical propagation to hot replicas is within seconds-to-minutes; to cold/offsite snapshot indexing it is processed at the next incremental snapshot job. Incremental jobs run hourly by default, but offsite snapshot consolidation runs in nightly batches. Practically: snapshot copies created before T0 will still contain the data until their TTL expires; snapshots created after T0 will not include the deleted objects.

2) Expunge/gc cadence- We run expunge in two stages: a tombstone-stage (logical delete) and an expunge-stage (physical deletion). Logical tombstones are immediate; expunge runs in scheduled windows (customer-configurable but default: weekly window with a 72-hour expunge job). There’s then a final sweep expunge that consolidates across replicas; because of cross-region replication lag and backlog, we recommend a 7–14 day buffer for contractual language to cover maximum propagation.

3) Legal hold- When a legal hold is set, GC/expunge jobs add a hold exception and those objects are skipped until hold is removed. This hold flag is authoritative and replicated like other metadata. Holds affect both hosted snapshots and Dedicated pools for Private customers (if hold set in control plane).

4) KMS & key destruction implications- If you elect customer-managed keys and subsequently destroy the key, snapshots encrypted with that key cannot be recovered. We retain metadata that the snapshot existed and can provide signed audit logs proving the encryption key and deletion timestamps, but we cannot decrypt without the key. If you need the ability to restore for audits, do not destroy keys until the retention/hold obligations are fully resolved.

5) Recommended contractual windows- For SOW language we typically suggest:
  - "Snapshot immutability window": snapshots created prior to deletion may retain copies until snapshot TTL; define TTL explicitly (e.g., 30/90/365 days).
  - "Expunge propagation window": allow up to 14 days for deletion propagation across DR/offsite copies and final expunge to complete.
  - "Legal hold exclusion": legal holds supersede TTL/expunge.
